statement: AI can do the first pass of screening or extraction, but a human still has to verify the output before it enters a review.
The hard part of a literature review is synthesis - connecting papers into an argument - and that is the part AI does worst.
Any AI-assisted review should state which tool did which step, so readers can judge the process.
Requiring three different models to agree before accepting a screening decision is worth the extra cost.
If an AI agent matches expert performance on literature search, insisting on human search is nostalgia rather than rigor.
Missing a few relevant studies is an acceptable price for screening 200 abstracts in 20 minutes.
Students should have to do one literature review by hand before they are allowed to use AI for one.
Published literature reviews are becoming obsolete because you can as LLMs to generate a lit review for you at any time.
We don't need to read scientific papers anymore, AI can read it for us.
AI can make the early stages of a literature review, but relying on it in the later stages may lead us to miss important studies.
AI makes things cognitively easy that should be difficult. For example, finding relevant articles, connecting findings, and conceptualizing.
AI tools can complement established review methods; it does not replace comprehensive searching, formal screening, or critical appraisal.
